title: Anaerobic respiration; Link reaction and Krebs cycle
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AQA A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: RS02#t2 term and clue written for the game; RS02#t4 term and clue written for the game; RS02#t3 term and clue written for the game; RS02#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: RS02#N.3a, RS04#N.3a, RS02#N.5, RS04#N.11a.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Matrix
items.clue: The fluid enclosed by the inner mitochondrial membrane.

items.label: Outer membrane
items.clue: Smooth boundary layer that encloses the whole mitochondrion.

items.label: Intermembrane space
items.clue: Narrow gap between the outer and inner boundaries of a mitochondrion.

items.label: Cristae
items.clue: Folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane, holding the electron carriers.

questions.stem: What happens to pyruvate in the link reaction of aerobic cell respiration?

options.text: It enters the Krebs cycle directly, where it combines with oxaloacetate to form citrate.
It reacts with oxygen in the matrix, forming carbon dioxide and a two-carbon acetyl group that enters the cycle.
It is oxidised and decarboxylated to a 2C acetyl group, which coenzyme A carries to the Krebs cycle.
It is bound by coenzyme A, the enzyme that catalyses its conversion into citrate in the matrix.

questions.explanation: Pyruvate loses carbon dioxide (decarboxylation) and hydrogen (oxidation, reducing NAD). The acetyl group is bound to coenzyme A and transferred to the cycle.

questions.stem: During intense exercise, muscle cells convert pyruvate to lactate. What is the purpose of this conversion?

options.text: To release extra ATP from pyruvate once the mitochondria have stopped working.
To oxidise pyruvate so that more reduced NAD is available to the cell.
To convert pyruvate into a form able to enter the mitochondria.
To regenerate NAD so that glycolysis can continue producing ATP.

questions.explanation: Reducing pyruvate to lactate turns reduced NAD back to NAD. Glycolysis, which needs NAD, continues with a net two ATP per glucose.

questions.stem: One acetyl group enters the Krebs cycle and oxaloacetate is regenerated. Which account of one turn of the cycle is correct?

options.text: Two decarboxylations give off carbon dioxide, four dehydrogenations reduce carriers, one ATP forms.
Two carbon dioxide molecules form when oxygen oxidises the carbon atoms of the acetyl group directly.
Each of the four oxidations forms one ATP directly, so the cycle yields most of the cell's ATP supply.
Only decarboxylation occurs, since no oxygen enters the matrix to oxidise any of the cycle's intermediates.

questions.explanation: Per turn, two carbons leave as carbon dioxide, four oxidations by removal of hydrogen produce reduced carriers (mainly reduced NAD), and one ATP forms directly.

questions.stem: Crucian carp can survive for months in ice-covered ponds with no oxygen. In these conditions their muscle cells convert pyruvate to ethanol and carbon dioxide, and the ethanol leaves through the gills. Which statement about this anaerobic respiration is correct?

options.text: It takes place inside the mitochondria, which is where the ethanol is made.
All its ATP comes from glycolysis: far less per glucose than aerobic respiration.
Converting pyruvate to ethanol releases extra ATP, which is why the fish survives.
It still uses the small amount of oxygen that remains dissolved in the pond water.
